summary:
Guadeloupe stands under France's national framework: French criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute, the marriage regime and the rules on identity documents apply here as they do in the metropole. Same-sex marriage is available, gender-identity discrimination is prohibited, and legal gender recognition follows the simplified French procedure. No legal penalty attaches to trans existence.

Custodial settings are the documented risk area. A BuzzFeed News report of January 2018 found that in French prisons, whose rules govern detention in Guadeloupe, the placement of trans women follows the legal gender recorded on the incarceration papers, which may not correspond to the person's presentation; in practice, assignment is said to weigh the individual's best interests, with individual cells or placement in more welcoming wings used where possible. The national preventive mechanism, the CGLPL, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, reporting serious violations of fundamental rights across French detention facilities and drawing on some forty referrals received since 2010.

Support infrastructure has expanded. Guadeloupe's first dedicated LGBT+ centre, the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened on 24 April 2024, offering reception, support and guidance for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities; it was driven by a federation of Guadeloupean associations. During the opening, the minister responsible for family affairs and diversity, Aurore Bergé, announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination in Guadeloupe, with structures adapted to overseas territories.

Community organisation is visible and growing. A September 2023 interview with organisers of Secret's Out described community members increasingly reconciling their lives with their orientation, with activism advancing after Martinique, alongside the work of Amalgame Humani's. In 2025, Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova partnered on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe. A 2023 local mapping of anti-LGBT violence exists, and organisers describe a gap between legal protection and lived experience.
tangentialFactors:
The protections in force are national French statutes rather than territory-specific legislation, so any change in French law on gender recognition, discrimination or family law would apply in Guadeloupe without a separate local vote.

Guadeloupe's trajectory on community visibility is described by local organisers as following Martinique, the neighbouring overseas department, where LGBT activism developed earlier.

The CGLPL opinion concerns places of detention across France as a whole; its findings are not specific to Guadeloupe's prisons, though the same national detention rules govern them.

Ministerial attention to the April 2024 centre opening signals political salience of inclusion policy in the overseas departments, alongside the national programme for such centres.
localsOnly:
Residents have access to the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion for reception, support and guidance, run by a federation of local associations, and to recurring community programming organised by groups including Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova.

Residents benefit from the full French legal toolkit: anti-discrimination remedies, hate-crime provisions in criminal law, and the administrative procedure for changing gender markers on official documents.

People facing gender-based violence can draw on the structures announced by the French government for overseas territories, though the specific form those adapted structures take in Guadeloupe is not detailed in the available sources.

Local organisers report a 2023 mapping exercise of anti-LGBT violence in the territory, an instrument intended for community and policy use rather than visitor guidance.
outOfScopeNotes:
The gap organisers describe between legal protection and lived experience is asserted in interview material without quantified evidence; the 2023 mapping's findings are not published in the sources available here, so the scale of anti-trans violence in Guadeloupe remains unresolved.

Whether trans detainees in Guadeloupe's own correctional facilities have been placed according to the criteria described in the 2018 reporting, and whether the CGLPL's findings apply to local facilities specifically, is not sourced.

The measures announced by Aurore Bergé in April 2024 are described as commitments; their implementation status in Guadeloupe is not documented in the inventory.

No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa screening, customs questions about hormone medication, or healthcare access for trans visitors in Guadeloupe.
